The Futurama Theorem

LogicAlgorithmsCounting
Game: Some people's minds are mixed up between their bodies. Put every mind back where it belongs, but no two bodies may swap minds twice, and every swap needs one of the two helpers X and Y.
How to play: Press one body, then another, to swap their minds. Take back the last swap if you need to.

Look for the math

In an episode of Futurama a machine swaps the minds of two bodies, but never the same two bodies twice. The show's writer, Ken Keeler, proved that two extra people, never swapped before, can always put every mind back. The game is a permutation problem.

Cycles and transpositions

Every mix-up splits into cycles, like (A B C): A's mind is in B’s body, B’s in C’s, C’s in A’s. A swap is a transposition. Three lemmas: swapping two neighbours in a cycle takes one of them out of it; swapping a cycle member with an outsider X puts X into the cycle; and (a x y b)(x b) = (a x)(b y). The logic test verified each as a product of permutations, for cycles up to length 8.

Does it always work?

The Futurama theorem says yes, for any number of people. The test did not rely on the proof alone: it went through every mix-up of 3 and of 4 people, and 120 random mix-ups of 5, 6 and 7, and found a sequence of swaps that involves X or Y and never repeats a pair; the game replayed each one. A mix-up of n people needs at least n minus the number of cycles swaps, plus two for each time a swap joins two cycles, which is how the search is organised. Press Show a solution to watch one (up to 7 people).

As in the applet, a pair of bodies can swap only once, a swap must include X or Y, Take back frees the pair, and the game is done when every mind is home.
